meta./en/food/cities/ayutthaya/: Ayutthaya food guide to boat noodles, grilled river prawns and roti sai mai, thin roti wrapped around sugar threads, with how river prawn prices vary by size and how to buy fruit near the ruins.
meta./en/food/cities/khon-kaen/: Khon Kaen food guide to Isan dishes: som tam and larb with sticky rice, sai krok Isan fermented sausage and au pla freshwater fish curry, with what to ask about plara and how to buy papaya.
meta./en/food/cities/hat-yai/: Hat Yai food guide to Hat Yai fried chicken with fried shallots and bak kut teh pork rib soup, the Chinese and Muslim food culture of Songkhla, and why a dish name cannot tell you if it is halal.
meta./en/food/dishes/pad-thai/: Pad Thai is Thailand's best-known stir-fried noodle dish with egg, tofu and tamarind sauce. Learn how it tastes, how to add lime and peanuts, and what to ask about dried shrimp if you avoid shrimp.
meta./en/food/dishes/tom-yum-kung/: Tom Yum Kung is a hot and sour shrimp soup scented with lemongrass, galangal and kaffir lime leaves. Learn how it tastes, how to order it with rice, and what its 2024 UNESCO listing means.
meta./en/food/dishes/green-curry/: Green curry, or kaeng khiao wan, is made with coconut milk, green curry paste, meat and vegetables, and it is still spicy. Learn how it tastes and how to ask about heat before you order.
meta./en/food/dishes/massaman/: Massaman curry is a rich Thai curry scented with cinnamon, cardamom and cloves, comparatively mild but not free of heat. Learn how it tastes and why its name cannot tell you if it is halal.
meta./en/food/dishes/mango-sticky-rice/: Mango sticky rice is a Thai dessert of ripe mango with coconut milk sticky rice, enjoyed after a meal. Learn how it tastes, how to eat mango and rice together and how to add the sauce slowly.
meta./en/food/dishes/khao-soi/: Khao soi is the northern Thai dish of egg noodles in coconut curry broth topped with crispy fried noodles. Learn how it tastes, how to choose chicken or beef, and why to eat the crisp noodles first.
meta./en/food/dishes/sai-ua/: Sai ua is a northern Thai sausage of pork, chilies, garlic and herbs, grilled and popular in Chiang Mai. Learn how it tastes, why to start with a small piece and how to eat it with sticky rice.
meta./en/food/dishes/nam-prik-ong/: Nam prik ong is a northern Thai dipping sauce of tomato, minced pork and chilies, eaten with vegetables and sticky rice. Learn how it tastes, how to pair it with sai ua and why it is not vegetarian.
meta./en/food/dishes/mi-hokkien/: Mi hokkien is a Phuket dish of thick yellow noodles stir-fried with seafood and sauce, shaped by Chinese food culture. Learn how it differs from mi hun and what to ask if you cannot eat seafood.
meta./en/food/dishes/mi-hun/: Mi hun is a Phuket dish of thin rice noodles best known with a pork rib broth, also found as mi hun ba chang. Learn how to eat the noodles and broth, and why skipping the broth does not avoid pork.
meta./en/food/dishes/o-aew/: O-aew is a Phuket dessert of jelly, sweet syrup and toppings served over ice, a cold break on a hot day in the old town. Learn how to spoon up ice and jelly and what to ask if you avoid ingredients.
meta./en/food/dishes/boat-noodles/: Boat noodles, or kuai tiao ruea, are noodles and meat in broth and famous in Ayutthaya. Learn how to choose noodles, meat and bowl size, and what to ask about meat, offal and seasoning in the broth.
meta./en/food/dishes/river-prawns/: Grilled river prawns are an Ayutthaya dish to share with rice. Learn why price changes with size and selling unit, how to ask if it is per prawn or by weight, and why the name does not prove origin.
meta./en/food/dishes/roti-sai-mai/: Roti sai mai is an Ayutthaya snack of thin roti wrapped around fine sugar threads, tied to local Muslim snack culture. Learn how it differs from ordinary roti, the pandan version and how to wrap it.
meta./en/food/dishes/som-tam/: Som tam is Isan's signature papaya salad, pounded with chilies and sour seasonings and eaten across Thailand. Learn how it tastes, when to ask about plara fish seasoning and how to cut the heat.
meta./en/food/dishes/larb/: Larb is an Isan meat salad of minced meat with toasted rice powder, lime and herbs, eaten with sticky rice. Learn how it tastes and why to order it cooked, since some larb uses raw meat.
meta./en/food/dishes/sai-krok-isan/: Sai krok Isan is an Isan sausage of fermented pork, rice and garlic, with a tang that sets it apart from northern sai ua. Learn how it tastes and how to eat the raw chilies served with it slowly.
meta./en/food/dishes/au-pla/: Au pla is a spicy, salty freshwater fish curry presented as a local dish of Khon Kaen. Learn how it differs from som tam and larb, what to ask about the fish and heat, and how to watch for bones.
meta./en/food/dishes/hat-yai-chicken/: Hat Yai fried chicken is a signature dish of Hat Yai, seasoned with garlic, coriander root and white pepper, with fried shallots. Learn how to eat it and why chicken alone is no halal proof.
meta./en/food/dishes/bak-kut-teh/: Bak kut teh is a Chinese-descended pork rib soup simmered with herbs, found in the Songkhla area. Learn how it tastes, why it is not called a Hat Yai original, and why it is not for pork avoiders.
meta./en/food/dishes/roti/: Thai roti is a street snack of cooked thin dough with sweet sauces like condensed milk or chocolate, sometimes with banana. Learn how to order it and how it differs from roti sai mai.
meta./en/food/dishes/watermelon-shake/: Taeng mo pan, the Thai watermelon shake, is watermelon blended with water and ice and sold as a street drink. Learn how it tastes, how to compare cup sizes and how to ask for less sugar.
meta./en/food/fruits/mango/: Mango in Thailand has a main season of March–May, with Nam Dok Mai and Maha Chanok varieties. Learn how ripe and green mango taste, how to cut it, and how price units differ for fruit and trays.
meta./en/food/fruits/durian/: Durian in Thailand has a main season of April–August, with Monthong, Chanee and Kan Yao varieties. Learn how it tastes, how to start small, and why to ask if the kg price includes the husk.
meta./en/food/fruits/mangosteen/: Mangosteen in Thailand has a main season of April–August. Learn how it tastes, how to open it, and why the Bangkok price of 40–60 baht per kg is not the weight of the flesh, since the skin is thick.
meta./en/food/fruits/rambutan/: Rambutan in Thailand is listed for harvest in April–August, and Nasan Rong Rian of Surat Thani is a regional GI fruit. Learn how it tastes, how to peel it and the Bangkok price of 50–60 baht per kg.
meta./en/food/fruits/longan/: Longan in Thailand has a main season of June–August, and Lamphun Biao Kiao longan is a regional GI fruit. Learn how it tastes, how to peel it, and the Bangkok price of 50–60 baht per kg.
meta./en/food/fruits/lychee/: Lychee in Thailand is listed for harvest in April–June, and Samut Songkhram Kom lychee is a regional GI fruit. Learn how to peel it, how it tastes, and why lychee drinks may not match fresh fruit.
meta./en/food/fruits/longkong/: Longkong in Thailand is listed for harvest in May–September, and Tha Yong Mat longkong is a regional GI fruit. Learn how it differs from longan, how to peel it and the Bangkok price of 40–50 baht/kg.
meta./en/food/fruits/pomelo/: Pomelo in Thailand has a main season of October–December and looks like a huge grapefruit. Learn how to peel it, why a prepared tray is easier, and why fruit and trays are hard to compare by weight.
meta./en/food/fruits/pineapple/: Pineapple in Thailand has a main season of April–July, and Si Thong pineapple of Trat is a regional GI fruit. Learn how it tastes, how to eat it, and the Bangkok price, 30–32 baht per kg.
meta./en/food/fruits/banana/: Thai banana is a fruit to enjoy all year, often priced by the bunch, and Kamphaeng Phet Kluai Khai is a regional GI fruit. See what to check on a bunch and Nam Wa at 40–50 baht per bunch in Bangkok.
meta./en/food/fruits/coconut/: Young coconut in Thailand is harvested all year, and the fragrant Nam Hom of Ban Phaeo is a regional GI fruit. Learn how to drink the water and eat the flesh, and why bottled water is priced apart.
meta./en/food/fruits/watermelon/: Watermelon in Thailand is harvested all year and enjoyed as taeng mo pan, blended with ice. Learn how to eat it, why fruit, slices and shake are priced apart, and the Bangkok price, 25–30 baht/kg.
meta./en/food/fruits/papaya/: Papaya in Thailand is harvested all year. Learn how ripe papaya, eaten soft and sweet, differs from the green papaya used in som tam, how to cut it, and the Bangkok price of 40–60 baht per kg.
meta./en/food/fruits/tamarind/: Sweet tamarind in Thailand has a main harvest listed from late December to February, and Phetchabun sweet tamarind is a regional GI fruit. Learn how to open the pod and remove fibers and seeds.
meta./en/food/fruits/mandarin/: Thai mandarin orange is in season October–February, and Nan golden orange is a green-skinned regional GI fruit. Learn how it tastes, why green is not unripe and the Bangkok price, 60–65 baht/kg.
meta./en/food/fruits/marian-plum/: Mayongchid, or Marian plum, is a plum mango family fruit with a Nakhon Nayok harvest listed for January–March. Learn how it tastes, how to cut it and remove the seed, and why to name the variety.
